query: For MnNiSi-based magnetic-refrigeration materials, what single intervention could improve mechanical performance while retaining a large magnetocaloric effect? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected changes relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Partial substitution of 15 at.% of Ni by Fe in bulk MnNiSi (yielding MnNi0.85Fe0.15Si) will create an in-situ ductile α-Fe secondary phase that toughens the alloy while preserving most of its magnetocaloric performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Arc-melted, homogenised, polycrystalline stoichiometric MnNiSi alloy that shows a large magnetocaloric effect (ΔS≈30 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ for Δµ₀H=5 T near 330 K) but is brittle (compressive plastic strain <1 %).
generation.intervention: Replace 15 at.% of Ni with Fe (MnNi0.85Fe0.15Si) followed by 1173 K / 24 h anneal and furnace cooling.
generation.conditions: Measurements on bulk samples in the temperature window 300–350 K under magnetic-field changes up to 5 T; room-temperature quasistatic compression tests.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a two-phase microstructure consisting of (1) the orthorhombic TiNiSi-type MnNiSi matrix and (2) ~10–20 vol.% ductile α-Fe precipitates located mainly along prior grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The ductile α-Fe bridges and arrests cracks and accommodates the transformation-induced strain, raising fracture toughness and plastic strain. Because the magnetocaloric response originates chiefly from the Mn-rich orthorhombic matrix, and Fe couples ferromagnetically with Mn, the isothermal entropy change is only modestly reduced.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with the baseline alloy, the Fe-substituted material will (a) exhibit ≥50 % higher compressive fracture strain (e.g., from <1 % to ≥1.5 %) or a similar relative increase in fracture toughness, while (b) retaining ≥85 % of the baseline ΔS (≥25 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ for Δµ₀H=5 T).
generation.baseline: Stoichiometric MnNiSi processed identically but without Fe addition.
generation.boundary: If Fe substitution exceeds ~25 at.% or if annealing is omitted, excessive α-Fe or disorder will reduce ΔS below 20 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and the hypothesis no longer applies.
generation.uncertainty: Moderate: exact α-Fe volume fraction and its distribution depend sensitively on cooling rate and may shift transformation temperatures, potentially altering ΔS beyond the 15 % tolerance.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two ingots: (1) MnNiSi (baseline) and (2) MnNi0.85Fe0.15Si, both arc-melted, homogenised at 1173 K for 24 h, furnace-cooled, and machined into 3 mm×4 mm×6 mm prisms. Perform (i) room-temperature uniaxial compression at 10⁻³ s⁻¹ to failure, recording stress–strain curves, and (ii) magnetisation-vs-temperature measurements (5 T→0 T) to obtain ΔS(T) via the Maxwell relation.
measurements: Compressive plastic strain to failure (or fracture toughness K_IC)
Isothermal entropy change ΔS at 330 K for Δµ₀H=0–5 T
Phase fractions via X-ray diffraction and SEM-EDS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if either (A) the Fe-substituted sample shows <20 % improvement in fracture strain (or toughness) over baseline, or (B) its ΔS is reduced by >15 % relative to baseline.
